docs.title: iii. Key takeaways
docs.text:
It appears like the new feature implementations were successfully implemented by Bob's agentic sidebar! Fully in accordance with the full Plan → review → new conversation → Agent workflow best practices we established earlier.

In the following section (Module 3 | Tailor), you will explore and go hands-on with topics covering ways to "teach" Bob your organization's particular codebase, encode that understanding with an organization's standards and rules, and shape Bob's behavior using Custom Modes.

docs.title: The Context Window | Keeping Bob reliable at scale
docs.text: MODULE 4 | SCALE & EXTEND

docs.title: i. Keeping Bob reliable at scale
docs.text:
Across this module, you will first look under the hood at the context window mechanics that make Bob tick. Arguably, the context window might be the single biggest factor in keeping Bob's output at the highest quality across the most ambitious tasks. The habits and best practices that developers (you) adopt in maximizing the utility of this resource can have tremendous impacts on the quality of work that Bob is able to perform.

Afterwards, you'll take Bob out of the IDE entirely and into the Terminal console: Bob Shell. This programmatic interface for Bob unlocks automation, scripting, and parallelized workstreams.

Finally, you will experiment with connecting Bob to your existing systems through Model Context Protocol (MCP), the open source standard that lets Bob interact directly with the external tools your teams use daily. Governance remains paramount at this stage. As the human-in-the-loop and final arbiter of control, you must decide what context Bob carries, what credentials it holds, and which tools it is permissioned to reach.

AI MATURITY CURVE

By the end of Module 3 | Tailor, IBM Bob knew nearly every facet about your project, adhered to your organization's coding standards, and had adapted itself to each role on your team — and all of that was committed to the repository, shared, and automatically enforced. The final stage along the AI Maturity Curve journey reflects the two things that separate a promising demo from a dependable enterprise partner: staying reliable on the largest, longest-running workloads; ultimately, connecting to everything else that your organization already runs today.

In other words, addressing the enterprise challenges of Scale and Extensibility.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
The context window represents the total amount of information a large language model (LLM) can hold "in mind" during a single session or conversation. It is also sets the potential limit of how much work any given LLM can perform: the larger the context window, the more substantial scale of task that can be performed (and likely the higher quality output that can be achieved.) Understanding how a context window "fills" (and how to manage these finite resources effectively) is what separates a polished technology demonstration from one that degrades in quality halfway through the work.

This lesson is conceptual. There are no steps to run, but the habits it instills will shape every other interaction you have with Bob. In the following chapter, you will go hands-on once again and put this theory in practice.

docs.title: iii. What is a context window?
docs.text:
The models powering Bob offer a context window of 270,000 tokens — and this number is continuing to expand with new releases. Every conversation begins with that full capacity available, and it holds everything: instructions, file contents, conversation history, and Bob's own responses. Once the window fills, the oldest content within the context window has to either be dropped from memory or summarized to make room.

At the start of every conversation, content loads in a predictable sequence:

ORDER OF OPERATIONS CONTENT NOTES 1 Bob system prompt Hidden from the user; contains Bob's core instructions 2 Mode description The definition of the currently active Bob Mode (Agent, Plan, Ask, etc.) 3 Rules Content from all files in .bob/rules/ 4 MCP tool definitions Can be very large, depending on the number and complexity of connected MCP servers 5 Conversation messages User prompts and Bob's responses 6 File reads and writes Contents of files Bob reads or produces during the conversation

THE IMPORTANCE OF GOVERNANCE

MCP tool definitions deserve special attention. The more external servers connected via MCP to Bob, the more rapidly that a significant slice of Bob's context window is exhausted before the user (you) send even a single message. This is why the importance of good governance and planning are emphasized again and again throughout this module.

docs.title: iv. What happens when the context window is full?
docs.text:
Reaching the 270,000-token limit doesn't stop Bob or throw an error. Instead, a new conversation starts automatically in the background.

Bob generates a summary of the previous conversation or session, and then that summary is pre-pended as context to the new conversation. Bob will carry on its responses and workflow seamlessly. The process is invisible to you — but it has real consequences for quality and cost, and that is precisely why it's worth understanding how to govern this resource allocation in detail.

The first cost: summarization is lossy. When a conversation overflows the context window size and needs to be summarized, the precision and fidelity of the original conversation are compromised. Specific technical details, intermediate reasoning, and nuanced context can be lost within the new Bob conversation. If a critical constraint or edge case was discussed early on, it may not persist into the summary or new conversation's memory, and as such implementation quality can suffer.

The second cost: quality degrades above roughly 100,000 tokens. Models don't hold uniform quality across the full range; as the window fills, responses noticeably decline, particularly past the ~100,000-token mark. A conversation using 50,000 tokens will generally produce better output than one using 180,000, all other things being equal. And because tokens are the unit of consumption (measured in Bob Coins), longer conversations and larger file reads also simply cost more of the finite context window. Less context used equates both better output and lower costs.

docs.title: iv. Context window strategies: persistent artifacts
docs.text:
The most effective way to manage all of this is with persistent artifacts. This strategy and pattern of work can be achieved in a variety of ways. Generally speaking, the most effective route involves breaking complex tasks into smaller, more discrete steps. This is, of course, a balancing act: one of the strengths of large language models (LLM) is being able to chain complex tasks into a single request or line of thought; however, the "art" in good prompting is balancing the complexity of those requests with the context window size available to the LLM.

One way to achieve this is having each step in an otherwise-complex workfow produce a saved output (such as a file on disk) and starting a new conversation for each major step with reference to those saved outputs. This keeps conversations and instructions contained in terms of size: no single conversation balloons too large in scale and every important decision is preserved as a durable file that you can point back to later.

You have already seen this in action. The seat-class feature from Module 2 was built exactly this way:

CONVERSATION TASK OUTPUT 1 Plan the feature seat-class-implementation-plan.md, seat-class-architecture.md 2 Implement based on plan Code changes across frontend, backend, and database

The implementation conversation consumed just 88,000 of 270,000 tokens— comfortably within the high quality range —because the two-conversation split kept the planning discussion from competing with the implementation for space.

CONTEXT WINDOW GUIDELINES

Several practical guidelines to keep in mind as you work with Bob's (and any other LLM's) context window:

  1. Start new conversations when you switch tasks (planning shouldn't bleed into implementation)
  2. Give preference to direct file references (@/path/to/file) over copy & paste from clipboard contents
  3. Keep MCP configurations lean, since every server's definitions will ultimately eat into the context window with every invocation
  4. Monitor token usage to see which interactions are most expensive and adjust accordingly.

docs.title: v. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• As of June 2026, Bob's context window is 270,000 tokens and every new conversation starts with a full allocation of this 270K capacity
  • Context fills according to a hierarchy: system prompts → mode description → rules → MCP tools → messages → file reads/writes
  • When the context window is exhausted, Bob auto-summarizes and seamlessly creates a new conversation under the covers (but summarization can be lossy)
  • Quality noticeably degrades beyond ~100,000 tokens
  • The persistent artifacts pattern (plan → save → new conversation → implement) is the primary strategy for managing context
  • The less context window that is consumed, the higher quality of outputs and the lower costs for generation

In the following section, you will step away from theory (and the Bob IDE altogether) to go hands-on with the Bob Shell programmatic interface.

docs.title: Bob Shell | Moving beyond the IDE
docs.text: MODULE 4 | SCALE & EXTEND

docs.title: i. Moving beyond the IDE
docs.text:
Everything so far has lived inside the IDE. Bob Shell brings the same core capabilities to a terminal — a keyboard-driven, command-line form factor installed separately from the VS Code extension and runnable in any standard terminal. For developers who live in the terminal, it unlocks workflows that are difficult or impossible in the IDE: headless automation, scripting, and running several Bob instances in parallel.

This is what taking Bob to enterprise scale looks like in practice.

ADDITIONAL DOCUMENTATION

Heads-up: completing this lesson may require additional guidance from IBM Bob's full product documentation to install Bob Shell. Detailed documentation is available from IBM.com

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
The Bob IDE and Bob Shell are complementary vectors for working with IBM Bob. In practice, you will discover that many workflows run both the Bob IDE and Bob Shell side-by-side. Some additional points of comparison on where and when to leverage either (or both) interfaces:

USE CASE BOB IDE BOB SHELL Visual file exploration Better Limited Keyboard-driven workflows Good Excellent Automation and scripting Not supported Supported (headless mode) Parallel instances Difficult Trivial Getting started Easier Steeper learning curve

docs.title: iii. Three reasons to reach for Bob Shell
docs.text:
1. Keyboard efficiency. Bob Shell removes mouse-driven interaction entirely — navigating files, issuing commands, reviewing output, and prompting Bob all happen through the keyboard. For developers who have internalized terminal workflows, the path from thought to action is faster, and the efficiency compounds; many adopt Bob Shell as a full daily-driver replacement for the IDE once it's familiar.

  2. Parallelization. Because Bob Shell runs in a terminal, multiple independent instances can run at once — one per tab, pane, or multiplexer window — which is trivial to set up compared with any IDE-based approach. You might run the IDE sidebar for exploratory work while one shell instance implements a backend change, another writes tests for a separate component, and a third generates documentation. Tasks with no shared state are the ideal candidates.

  3. Headless mode. Bob Shell supports a headless mode where input is piped directly to Bob rather than entered interactively. This single capability turns Bob into a programmable component rather than just an interactive assistant. Pipe compiler output to it for diagnosis, pipe log files to it for incident triage, generate summaries or reports as part of a script, or let it attempt minor fixes autonomously and escalate the complex ones. For example:

    cat error.log | bob "explain this"

    A NOTE ON SAFETY

    Governance, as always, is paramount. By default, Bob Shell applies stricter auto-approval settings than the Bob IDE. For example, file writes and shell commands require explicit confirmation by the user. The stricter default behavior is deliberate given that Bob Shell is often used in environments (servers, continuous integration pipelines, or scripts) where unreviewed changes can carry broader consequences, compared to within the constraints of a local IDE session.

    QUIZ QUESTION - IBM BOB LEVEL 4

    If you are planning to pursue IBM Bob Level 4 accreditation, what is rendered on-screen or returned within a console as a result of this step are likely referenced as part of a multiple-choice question. It is strongly recommend that you record to a notebook (for reference later) details about how the Bob Shell being used from a script with no interactive session at all.

docs.title: iv. Getting started and navigation tips
docs.text:
Once installed, invoke Bob Shell by running:

bob

On first use, Shell prompts for IBM login credentials. After successfully authenticating, it behaves much like the Bob IDE Chat interface: you type natural-language prompts directly at into the Shell prompt, with Bob reading and modifying files in the current working directory based upon those requests.

INVOKING REGULAR (NON-BOB) SHELL COMMANDS

Within a Bob Shell session, prefix any command with ! to invoke regular (non-Bob) shell commands. For example:

!git diff
!cat README.md
!ls -la

QUIZ QUESTION - IBM BOB LEVEL 4

If you are planning to pursue IBM Bob Level 4 accreditation, what is rendered on-screen or returned within a console as a result of this step are likely referenced as part of a multiple-choice question. It is strongly recommend that you record to a notebook (for reference later) details about what character you use to prefix any Bob Shell commands.

The net result for the developer (you) is being able to alternate between AI-assisted workflows (with Bob Shell) and standard bash shell operations seamlessly, without needing to leave or create a separate session.

docs.title: v. Hands-on: Installing and using Bob Shell
docs.text:
Follow the video for a full walkthrough: Chapter 4.2: Bob Shell [IBM Bob L3]

To begin, you will first need to follow the directions below for setting up Bob Shell within your Windows or MacOS environment. Follow the instruction set specific to your operating system.

Afterwards, you will go hands-on with using Bob Shell to programmatically send a prompt, drop into Shell Mode, and explore various commands.

  1. Open a new Terminal window by pressing the Terminal button at the top of Bob IDE.

    Alternatively, you can use the Terminal application on MacOS or the PowerShell application on Windows.

  1. Click New Terminal to launch a new console instance.

  1. To download the Bob Shell to your local machine, follow the instruction set below that matches your machine's operating system.

    MAC OR LINUX

    1. Copy the following command and paste into the Terminal console, then hit Enter to execute: 

      curl -fsSL https://bob.ibm.com/download/bobshell.sh | sudo bash

    2. You will be prompted for your machine's system password to complete the install. For security, no characters appear on screen as you type — but your input is being registered.

    3. Wait for the Terminal console to report back a successful installation of the Bob Shell. The message should look similar to the following: 

      bobshell x.x.x has been succesfully installed
You can now run: bob

    4. When ready, proceed to Step 4.

    WINDOWS OS

    1. Copy the following command and paste into the PowerShell console, then hit Enter to execute: 

      powershell -ep Bypass 'irm -Uri "https://bob.ibm.com/download/bobshell.ps1" | iex'

    2. Wait for the PowerShell console to report back a successful installation of the Bob Shell. The message should look similar to the following: 

      bobshell x.x.x has been succesfully installed
You can now run: bob

    3. When ready, proceed to Step 4.

  1. With the Bob Shell now successfully installed, copy and paste the following instruction into the console and hit Enter:

    bob

  1. The console will launch an external "Log in to IBM" page via your web browser.

    Complete the SSO sign-in using your w3ID credentials (also tied to your IBM Bob account.)

  1. Once signed in, you will be redirected to an "Authentication Successful!" page.

    You may safely close the web browser at this time.

  1. If this is your first time using Bob Shell, there's a small amount of configuration and bookkeeping to do beforehand.

    If prompted to accept the license agreement, review the contents and then type Y (followed by Enter) if you agree to the terms and conditions.

  1. When prompted to connect the Bob IDE to Bob Shell, use the arrow keys to highlight option 1. Yes (or type 1), and then press Enter to execute the command.

    ERROR: Failed to automatically enable IDE integration...

    If you receive this error:

    • Locate the currently-running process within the Terminal sidebar and press the bin icon to terminate it
    • Create a new Terminal console selecting Terminal > New Terminal from the top-line menu bar
    • Return to Step 4 and execute the steps a second time

  1. Within the Terminal console, a Welcome to Bob Shell splash screen will appear to confirm a successful connection has been established to the service.

    Scroll down until you reach the input field, denoted by the > ("greater than") brace.

  1. To test functionality, copy and paste the following prompt into the input field, then hit Enter to execute:

    check the readme and see if you can make any improvements

  1. In the same way that it did using the Agentic Sidebar within the Bob IDE, the Bob Shell narrates its progression through a Todo List as it executes upon the work.

    • Occasionally, Bob will ask for approval to complete tasks or actions as operates
    • The difference with Bob Shell is such check-ins with the human-in-the-loop happen via the Terminal console

  1. If asked for approvals, Bob Shell will present you with a numerated list as you saw previously.
    • Either use the arrows on your keyboard to move up and down the list, or press the corresponding number on your keyboard, to highlight one of the options
    • Confirm the selection by hitting Enter
    • Recommended that in all cases (for the hands-on lab) you opt for: 
      1. Yes, allow once

  1. The diff view captured in the screenshot below highlights Bob's proposed updates to the README.md file.

    As before: red highlights denote content marked for removal; green highlights denote content scheduled to be added.

  1. Prefixing any input into the Bob Shell console with an exclamation mark ! drops Bob Shell into shell mode (akin to a bash shell), where you can run ordinary shell commands.

    Test this by copy and pasting the following command into the Terminal console, then hit Enter to execute. 

    !cat README.md

    The cat (concatenate) command is used to view, create, and combine file contents directly from the console.

  1. As a result of executing the cat command, the Terminal console simply prints the README.md contents to the window.

    EXITING ! SHELL MODE

    Note that the ! exclamation marker remains on the left-hand side of the Terminal console. This indicates that the console remains in the generic shell mode.

    To exit generic shell mode, and return to the Bob Shell, press Esc at any time.

  1. Next, try using the git diff ... command to compare differences across the working copy of README.md (on your machine) and the version tracked within the local Git repository (typically the last commit.)

    Copy and paste the following instruction into the console, then press Enter to execute. 

    git diff README.md

    Take note of the + and - symbols on the left-side edge of each line: these denote changed lines between the two versions (indicating a new line added or existing line removed, respectively.)

  1. To exit generic shell mode, and return to the Bob Shell, press Esc at any time.

    Press Esc now to return to the Bob Shell, where you will investigate more of the commands available before progressing to the next chapter.

  1. There are a multitude of commands and operations you can perform using the Bob Shell, which we have just barely scratched the surface of here.

    Copy and paste the following command, followed by Enter, to display a full list of ways that you can interact with the Bob Shell: 

    /help

docs.title: vi. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Bob Shell provides the same capabilities as Bob IDE, but via a programmatic console
  • Invoke the Bob Shell with bob; use the ! prefix for normal shell commands within a session
  • Exit the normal shell (!) shell mode and return to Bob Shell by typing Esc
  • Auto-approval is strict by default in Bob Shell, requiring you to confirm actions as prompted

CORE BENEFITS OF BOB SHELL

  1. Keyboard efficiency: faster for Terminal-native developers once the interface is learned
  2. Headless mode: cat file | bob "prompt" enables automation, pipeline integration, and scripted workflows
  3. Parallelization: multiple Bob Shell instances can run simultaneously for independent tasks

To conclude the hands-on modules, you will next examine Bob's open standards Model Context Protocol (MCP) as a means for connecting Bob to everything else within your enterprise.

docs.title: Extending with MCP | Connecting Bob to everything
docs.text: MODULE 4 | SCALE & EXTEND

docs.title: i. Connecting everything back to Bob
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is what connects IBM Bob to the rest of your business and the systems your organization spans: a standardized interface that lets LLM-powered applications reach external tools, services, and data sources through one consistent integration layer. Any external service that can provide an MCP server can potentially serve as another endpoint for Bob to work with. This is the final (and most consequential) step in scaling Bob across an enterprise- making Bob a participant in the systems your teams already use —and serves as an effective capstone to the work you've performed thus far.

THE FULL JOURNEY ALONG THE AI MATURITY CURVE

This final module completes your journey along the AI Maturity Curve. Before continuing on, step back and look at the shape of what you've done: - You began with Bob finishing your lines and predicting your next edit (Module 1 | Assist) - You handed Bob whole features to build from an approved plan (Module 2 | Delegate) - You taught Bob about your project structure and your organization's standards, reinforcing that learning until Bob behaved like a teammate (Module 3 | Tailor) - Finally, you made Made reliable at scale and connected to the systems your enterprise already runs (Module 4 | Scale & Extend)

A common thread across all of these modules and discussions has been the core value that the developer stays in control. Only the stakes changed (and escalated) across the journey from the nascent phases to the right-most portions of the curve. At Assist, control was apparent — the user (you) accepting each suggestion in sequence with a high degree of oversight. At Delegate, it was approving the plans that Bob put in place and trusting it to carry on the work beyond that point. At Tailor, it was encoding the rules and committing them to repositories that would ensure Bob adhered to your coding and organizational standards. Currently, at the Scale & Extend phase, trust becomes more about governing context, credentials, and tool access.

Follow this progression with any conversation or demonstration you have with clients about IBM Bob. Don't limit your planning to only a parade of features. Build out the storyline presented here to demonstrate a trustworthy path by which a team grows into working with an AI partner, without ever feeling like they've relinquished control or made shortcuts to their organization's established ways of winning.

docs.title: ii. What is MCP?
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) defines an open standards interface for connecting large language model (LLM) applications to external systems. Before it existed, wiring an LLM to an external tool meant building a custom connection layer for each potential endpoint — a significant, inconsistent level of effort that varied across teams and organizations. MCP replaces those old methods with a single protocol, both-sides implementation: once a service offers an MCP server, any MCP-compatible client (Bob included) can connect to it immediately, with no custom integration work.

MCP originated at Anthropic and has since been transferred to the Linux Foundation, making it a vendor-neutral, openly governed standard. This governance, more than anything else, is what has accelerated its widespread adoption across the industry. Most major external services and developer tools now ship MCP servers, creating an extensive ecosystem of ready-to-use integrations.

MCP servers are configured in Bob's settings through a JSON configuration file.

The simplified flow is as follows:

  1. Open Bob settings via the three-dot menu (⋯),
  2. Navigate to MCP Servers
  3. Add the server configuration in JSON
  4. Supply credentials as required

Most services publish their own configuration snippets within their official documentation. Furthermore, Bob itself can insert the JSON for you, handling indentation and brackets automatically.

How you handle credentials is a governance decision in itself:

METHOD DESCRIPTION USE CASE Inline with config Personal access token written directly in the JSON file Quick setup, local development only Environment variable Token stored as an OS environment variable, referenced in config Cleaner setup, avoids token in config file Context forage Open source MCP gateway for managing complex, multi-server setups Teams, production environments, multiple credentials

USING MCP TOOLS

MCP tools are available only in Bob's Agent Mode. With Agent Mode active, Bob automatically recognizes the tools exposed by every configured server and invokes them in response to natural-language requests.

No special syntax is quired required. Bob simply decides which MCP tools to call based on the task you describe.

The GitHub MCP server shows how much a single integration can add:

  • Configuration: paste GitHub's configuration snippet into the JSON config, then add a personal access token whose permissions match the operations Bob will perform (reading issues, creating commits, adding comments, closing issues)
  • Agent Mode capabilities enabled: with Agent Mode active, Bob can list and read issues, create commits and push changes, add comments, close issues, and link commits to issues
  • Testing: a token with insufficient permissions will simply cause the affected operation to fail and Bob will report the permission error so that you know to update the token

Strung together, Bob's Agent Mode capabilities make a complete issue-resolution loop possible entirely through natural language expressions. A full development cycle— from issue to closed resolution —is possible, without ever leaving the Bob interface:

  • Ask Bob to list open issues (Bob will call the GitHub MCP tool to retrieve them)
  • Describe the one issue to fix (Bob reads the relevant code and implements the change)
  • Instruct Bob to commit and push the fixed code (Bob calls the right MCP tools and git commands)
  • Comment (via Bob, at your behest) on the issue with a link to the commit and close the issue.

And GitHub is just one server in a fast-growing ecosystem that already spans version control and code review platforms, project management and issue-tracking tools, databases and data services, cloud infrastructure providers, and internal enterprise systems. In practice, most of the external integrations a development team relies upon can be connected to Bob through MCP, with no custom development required.

docs.title: iii. Key takeaways
docs.text:
WANT TO GO HANDS-ON WITH MCP?

IBM Bob's Model Context Protocol capabilities are extensive and worth a proper deep dive. To that end, the IBM Enablement team has been hard at work crafting a separate Level 3 series of hands-on labs dedicated exclusively to MCP, the IBM Bob Marketplace, and the synergies of such a technology stack with other parts of IBM's portfolio (including IBM Technology Zone client-facing demos.)

Once published, the Level 3 courseware will be linked directly from here — as well as via other IBM Bob-related sales enablement channels. Stay tuned.

Let's review some key concepts:

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standardized interface for connecting Bob to external tools and services
  • Originated at Anthropic and is now governed by the Linux Foundation as a vendor-neutral standard
  • Primary value is coordination: a shared standard eliminates custom integration work
  • MCP servers are configured in Bob's settings as JSON (credentials can be inline, environment variables, or managed through Context Forage)
  • MCP tools require IBM Bob's Agent Mode to be enabled
  • GitHub MCP server allows Bob to list issues, create commits, push changes, add comments, and close issues through natural language prompts

From here, it's time to make Bob your own. Run these workflows against a codebase that you actually know and work with today, in front of the kind of client you actually serve. Apply the AI Maturity Curve methodology to ensure that your demonstration resonates and speaks to Bob's value with those audiences.

docs.title: init & agents.md | Teaching Bob your codebase
docs.text: MODULE 3 | TAILOR

docs.title: i. Teaching Bob your codebase
docs.text:
Across the first two modules (Assist and Delegate), Bob was put to work with minimal-to-no background or context about your codebase. Bob proved itself to be capable, but operating and working only from what it could read and infer based in the moment. Module 3 (Tailor) will change that approach markedly. Here you will teach Bob about your project and your standards, so that Bob begins behaving like a teammate who already knows how your team works.

There are three ways to tailor Bob which build on one another:

  1. Provide Bob with durable knowledge about your codebase (so it stops rediscovering your project from scratch with every invocation)
  2. Encode the standards Bob must always follow (so quality and conventions are enforced without needing to be re-typed)
  3. Shape Bob's behavior to fit each role on your team (so a product manager and a senior engineer each get the specialized version of Bob that they need).

Notice where control lives at this stage in the AI Maturity Curve. Whereas in Modules 1 and 2 you approved Bob's work as it happened, here in Module 3 you write the rules down— commit them to the repository —and have them applied automatically, every time, for everyone. Viewed another way: Bob, at this stage in your jouney, has progressed beyond delegated work towards tailored work. Bob's behaviors, capabilities, and understanding are now being attuned specifically to the workflow and personas engaging with it.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
Large language models (LLM) are stateless and therefore every new conversation, without intervening strategies or techniques, will begin with no memory of the last interaction. Left to its own devices, Bob would need to rediscover your codebase from scratch at the start of each interaction — an inefficient approach for a small project and an impractically cumbersome approach for a large one.

The /init command solves this challenge. It scans your project and generates a structured summary that Bob loads as persistent context for every new conversation. The /init command thus becomes the primary mechanism for giving Bob durable knowledge of your project's structure, conventions, and code. All without needing to re-read every file with each new invocation.

RUNNING /init

Initializing a project's context takes seconds and requires no additional configuration. To do so using IBM Bob:

  1. Open the agentic sidebar in Bob IDE
  2. Enter the slash command: /init
  3. Bob reads the relevant files in the project
  4. Bob generates the agents.md context file

You'll have plenty of opportunities to practice this yourself when the hands-on portion of Module 3 kicks off. Beforehand, however, it's important to understand more about the complementary agents.md file.

THE AGENTS.MD FILE

The primary output of the /init command is agents.md: a plain-text Markdown file placed in the project root directory.

Think of agents.md as onboarding documentation written for specifically for Bob. It provides a concise, actionable summary of everything Bob needs to understand about the project in order to work effectively with it. The documentation typically covers: the project's overview and purpose; its directory structure and key file locations; the technology stack and dependencies; architectural patterns and conventions; and development workflows.

From the point it is first introduced and defined, agents.md is automatically prepended to every new conversation a user has with Bob, ensuring the LLM has immediate project context without requiring any manual file read efforts.

MODE-SPECIFIC CONTEXT FILES

Alongside the main agents.md Markdown documentation, the /init command also generates context files tuned to each one of Bob's built-in Modes (which we examined in Module 2):

FILE MODE .bob/rules-agent/AGENTS.md Agent mode (formerly Code and Advanced modes) .bob/rules-ask/AGENTS.md Ask mode .bob/rules-plan/AGENTS.md Plan mode

Each mode-specific file extends the base context with what matters most for the successful operations of a given Mode. Context for Plan mode might emphasize architectural conventions, while Agent mode context would benefit from highlighting file structure and naming patterns.

docs.title: iii. Hands-on: generating your project context
docs.text:
The larger your codebase, the more valuable a well-maintained AGENTS.md asset becomes. On a small project, Bob could conceivably read every file each conversation; even so, having a pre-defined AGENTS.md is still more efficient than the read-everything alternative. On a large project, an AGENTS.md manifest becomes the backbone of the entire workflow. It provides detailed guidance for how Bob should navigate the codebase, without exhausting the context window on file reads.

TIPS FOR /INIT AND AGENTS.MD

Execute the /init command after significant changes to ensure Bob picks up on any new modules or services, restructured directory trees, new framework, and so on. If there are instances where you (the administrator) want to capture context without performing an automated scan— or believe that an automated scan might miss some key elements, such as business rules or deployment conventions —then you may also edit the agents.md asset by-hand.

Let's give Bob durable knowledge of the Galaxium Travels codebase by running the /init command and generating its AGENTS.md files.

  1. First, ensure that Bob has enabled Agent mode within the Agentic Sidebar.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar, type the following and hit Enter to execute:

    /init

    You may need to click Approve once (once or several times...) to permission access to the agents.md file before this summary appears.

    QUIZ QUESTION - IBM BOB LEVEL 4

    If you are planning to pursue IBM Bob Level 4 accreditation, what is rendered on-screen or returned within a console as a result of this step are likely referenced as part of a multiple-choice question. It is strongly recommend that you record to a notebook (for reference later) the names and directory locaton of the three mode-specific context files inside .bob that are created as a result of running the /init command.

AGENTS OF GALAXIUM TRAVELS

After execution of the /init command, Bob's Agent mode will examine key front-end and back-end (service) files within the Project directory, ultimately writing a total of four files.

AGENTS.md — General guidance

  • Commands require running from specific subdirectories (pytest from booking_system_backend/, npm from booking_system_frontend/)
  • Single-test syntax with full pytest class path
  • The dual REST+MCP architecture on a single port

.bob/rules-agent/AGENTS.md — Coding gotchas

  • No seats_available column — test fixtures in the repo use an old column name that no longer exists in the model; discovered only by reading both models.py and the tests
  • MCP tools bypass FastAPI DI — they call SessionLocal() directly, so tests must patch two places
  • verbatimModuleSyntax enforces import type for type-only imports
  • Cancellation is POST, not DELETE

QUIZ QUESTION - IBM BOB LEVEL 4

If you are planning to pursue IBM Bob Level 4 accreditation, what is rendered on-screen or returned within a console as a result of this step are likely referenced as part of a multiple-choice question. It is strongly recommend that you record to a notebook (for reference later) details about the "gotchas" associated with a cancellation (it's a POST, not a DELETE).

.bob/rules-ask/AGENTS.md — Context for questions

  • Backend tests are partially outdated (use the old seat model)
  • Frontend has zero tests
  • booking_time has no timezone suffix despite being UTC

.bob/rules-plan/AGENTS.md — Architecture constraints

  • Price multipliers are frontend-only — backend stores only the economy base price
  • SQLite with no migration framework (no Alembic)
  • seed.py runs on every startup — not safe for multi-worker deployments
  • No update endpoint for bookings — cancel+rebook is the only flow

docs.title: iv. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• LLMs are stateless by default: every conversation starts fresh, with no memory of the last session or chat
  • The /init command scans your project(s) and generates agents.md documentation, a context file that will subsequently be included with every new Bob conversation
  • AGENTS.md functions like onboarding documentation: a structured summary that Bob utilizes to navigate your project(s)
  • Mode-specific AGENTS.md files give targeted context for IBM Bob's Agent, Plan, and Ask modes
  • For large-scale projects, AGENTS.md is essential: Bob cannot feasibly read every file at the start of each conversation without exhausting its (sizeable) context window
  • Re-run the /init command after major changes to capture the latest context for project(s)

In the chapter ahead, you will examine strategies for encoding your organization's coding standards using Bob Rules.

docs.title: Bob Rules | Encoding your standards
docs.text: MODULE 3 | TAILOR

docs.title: i. Encoding Bob with your standards
docs.text:
If AGENTS.md can teach Bob what your project is, Rules teach Bob how you expect it to behave.

Rules are plain-text files containing instructions that apply to every conversation between users and Bob. Rules, therefore, provide a way for teams and individuals to enforce coding standards, communication preferences, workflow constraints, and custom behaviors — without requiring them to be reintroduced with every new chat prompt. Every file in the Rules folder is automatically injected into each conversation, across all Bob Modes (Agent, Plan, Ask, and any custom modes you create.)

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
A documentation standard keeps generated code consistently commented:

Always include concise `JSDoc` strings for every public function.

A communication-style rule shapes how Bob phrases responses and comments (useful for teams that prefer terse output):

Be very concise in your wording.

And one particularly powerful pattern is the internal monologue rule which instructs Bob to log a summary of every interaction:

Write a summary of every interaction into the folder `internal-monologue/`.
Name the file starting with a timestamp, followed by a concise description of the interaction.
Example: `2026-01-15_update-readme.md`

This singular rule produces a persistent record of everything Bob has done:

  • An audit trail of what changed across a project's codebase and when
  • Cross-section continuity that Bob can refer back to in future conversations
  • Team transparency in shared repositories, where the monologue details what each teammate has done with Bob

docs.title: iii. Project vs. global scope rules
docs.text:
Project-level rules apply only to the current project that Bob is engaged with and are stored within the following directory structure:

.bob/rules/

Drop any plain-text or Markdown file into this endpoint and Bob will guarantee that each artifact is ingested prior to the start of every conversation.

Global rules apply across all projects on the local machine that the Bob IDE is acting upon. Such rules live in a separate, user-level directory, the exact path of which depends on your local machine's operating system.

Rules from both locations can be combined and applied together:

SCOPE LOCATION USE CASE Project .bob/rules/ in project root Rules specific to one codebase (framework conventions, project documentation standards) Global User-level rules directory Rules that apply everywhere (internal monologue, personal communication preferences)

RULES ARE COMMITTED TO THE REPOSITORY

This is the heart of the Tailor stage in your progression towards the right-side of the AI Maturity Curve.

Project-level rules in .bob/rules/ are version-controlled, much in the same way as the actual project code. This means that Bob Rules that you define will automatically:

  • Propagate to every teammate who clones the shared repository
  • Performs changes to repositories as they go through normal code review processes
  • Tracked in git for trace-back on the complete version history.

The control that you manually exercised in Assist— which you then later entrusted with more autonomy to Bob in the Delegate phase —now becomes a durable, shared, and reviewable artifact in the Tailor phase of the journey.

docs.title: iv. Hands-on: setting standards with Bob Rules
docs.text:
1. Within the Bob IDE, click the Explorer tab.

    Locate the .bob directory, which should be positioned directly under the GALAXIUM-TRAVELS folder header.

    CAN'T FIND BOB?

    If no .bob directory appears within the project hierarchy, you need to run the /init command within the Agentic Sidebar and approve the generation steps. Follow the documentation from the previous chapter for more details.

  1. Right-click .bob to expose additional options.

    • From the drop-down menu, select New Folder...
    • Name the folder rules and press Enter to confirm

  1. Right-click the newly-created rules folder.

    Click New File... from the drop-down options.

  1. Name the file basic_rules.md and press Enter to confirm.

    QUIZ QUESTION - IBM BOB LEVEL 4

    If you are planning to pursue IBM Bob Level 4 accreditation, what is rendered on-screen or returned within a console as a result of this step are likely referenced as part of a multiple-choice question. It is strongly recommend that you record to a notebook (for reference later) details about the name of the file used to hold the three project rules.

  1. The file should automatically open within the Bob IDE, exposing its contents (which are empty for the time being.)

  1. First, verify that Bob's Agentic Sidebar is still set to Agent mode.

  1. Next, create a new session of the Agentic Sidebar to clear all previous context. Use the New Task (+) button in the top-right corner of the Agentic Sidebar to do so.

  1. When ready, copy & paste the entire contents of the prompt below into the Agentic Sidebar and press Enter to execute:

    Please add the following rules to @/.bob/rules/basic_rules.md and configure them so they work:
- Always include concise JSDoc strings for every public function.
- Be very concise in your wording.
- Write a summary of every interaction into the folder `internal-monologue/`.Name the file starting with a timestamp, followed by a concise description of the interaction. Example: 2026-01-15_update-readme.md

  1. Bob will prompt you for permission to execute on several different tasks, including the ability to write a file within .bob/rules/basic_rules.md Markdown document.

    Approve these requests. We will examine the contents shortly once all work on the original request has completed and these files have been fully updated.

  1. Bob will ask to construct three new rules for an internal-monologue/ folder, consisting of the following:

    • JSDoc / docstrings | new ## Coding Standards section requiring a concise JSDoc on every public TS function and a one-line docstring on every public Python function.
    • Concise wording | rule to keep all comments, docstrings, and prose brief.
    • Interaction logging | new ## Interaction Logging section instructing the agent to write a timestamped summary to internal-monologue/ after every interaction.

    Take note that these rules are in alignment with the earlier instruction given via the Agentic Sidebar request.

  1. The workflow is complete once the Agentic Sidebar reports back the following (or something similar): The internal-monologue/ folder was created with 2026-06-20_add-coding-rules.md as the first log entry.

    QUIZ QUESTION - IBM BOB LEVEL 4

    If you are planning to pursue IBM Bob Level 4 accreditation, what is rendered on-screen or returned within a console as a result of this step are likely referenced as part of a multiple-choice question. It is strongly recommend that you record to a notebook (for reference later) details about what appeared in the project root as the first result of the interaction-logging rule.

    At this point, you should inspect the contents of the .bob/rules/basic_rules.md to validate the generative steps taken by Bob. You may do so by: clicking the file shortcut directly within the Agentic Sidebar session; via the Explorer tab project directory tree; or review within the documentation below.

    .bob/rules/basic_rules.md

        # Project Instructions (AGENTS.md)

    # AGENTS.md

    This file provides guidance to agents when working with code in this repository.

    ## Project Overview
    Galaxium Travels — an interplanetary flight booking system. The backend also exposes an **MCP server** (mounted at `/mcp`) alongside the REST API, both served from the same FastAPI process on port 8080.

    ## Stack
    - **Backend**: Python/FastAPI + SQLAlchemy (SQLite) + FastMCP. Entry point: `booking_system_backend/server.py`, run via `python server.py`.
    - **Frontend**: React 19 + TypeScript + Vite + Tailwind CSS. Run via `npm run dev` (from `booking_system_frontend/`).

    ## Commands

    ### Backend (run from `booking_system_backend/`, with `.venv` active)
    ```bash
    # Setup
    python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install -r requirements.txt

    # Run server
    python server.py   # http://localhost:8080, Swagger at /docs, MCP at /mcp

    # Run all tests
    pytest

    # Run a single test function
    pytest tests/test_services.py::TestBookingService::test_book_flight_success -v

    # Run a single test file
    pytest tests/test_rest.py -v
    ```

    ### Frontend (run from `booking_system_frontend/`)
    ```bash
    npm run dev      # http://localhost:5173
    npm run build    # tsc -b && vite build
    npm run lint     # eslint .
    ```

    ### Start both together (from repo root)
    ```bash
    ./start.sh
    ```

    ## Critical Backend Patterns

    ### Error handling: return ErrorResponse, don't raise
    Service functions return `BookingOut | ErrorResponse` (or similar). **Never raise exceptions** from service layer — return an `ErrorResponse` instance instead. REST endpoints return these directly; MCP tools convert them to `raise Exception(result.details or result.error)`.

    ### Seat classes: exactly three, specific names
    Valid seat classes are `"economy"`, `"business"`, `"galaxium"`. The Flight model has three separate seat columns (`economy_seats`, `business_seats`, `galaxium_seats`). There is no generic `seats_available` column — the `SEAT_CLASS_MAP` in `services/booking.py` maps class names to column names.

    ### Timestamps are ISO strings, stored as String columns
    Both `departure_time`/`arrival_time` on Flight and `booking_time` on Booking are `String` columns (not DateTime). `booking_time` is written as `datetime.utcnow().isoformat()`.

    ### Pydantic schemas use `model_validate()`, not `from_orm()`
    All schemas that wrap ORM models use `class Config: from_attributes = True`. Construct them with `BookingOut.model_validate(obj)`, not `.from_orm()`.

    ### Tests use in-memory SQLite + monkeypatching
    `conftest.py` patches both `db.SessionLocal` and `server.SessionLocal` (the MCP tools use `SessionLocal` directly, bypassing FastAPI dependency injection). Each test gets a fresh DB; `seed()` is patched to a no-op.

    ## Critical Frontend Patterns

    ### API base URL from env
    Configure `VITE_API_URL` in `.env` (see `.env.example`). Defaults to `http://localhost:8080`.

    ### Error detection: check `response.success === false`
    Use the `isErrorResponse(response)` helper from `src/services/api.ts` to distinguish `ErrorResponse` from success types. It checks `response.success === false`.

    ### Seat class utilities: use `src/utils/seatClasses.ts`
    Use `getSeatClassPrice(basePrice, seatClass)` for price with multipliers (economy ×1, business ×1.5, galaxium ×2.5) and `getSeatCount(flight, seatClass)` to read per-class seat counts. **Price is stored as an integer (cents/whole units)**; `formatCurrency` in `src/utils/formatters.ts` formats it as USD.

    ### TypeScript strictness
    `tsconfig.app.json` enables `strict`, `noUnusedLocals`, `noUnusedParameters`, and `verbatimModuleSyntax`. All types live in `src/types/index.ts`.

    ### Tailwind custom tokens
    Use project-specific color tokens: `space-dark`, `space-blue`, `cosmic-purple`, `nebula-pink`, `alien-green`, `solar-orange`, `star-white`. Backgrounds: `bg-space-gradient`, `bg-cosmic-gradient`.

    ## Coding Standards

    ### JSDoc for every public function
    Always include a concise JSDoc comment on every public function (frontend TypeScript) and a one-line docstring on every public function (backend Python). Keep wording brief — one sentence is enough.

    ### Concise wording
    Be very concise in all code comments, docstrings, and prose. Prefer short, direct sentences.

    ## Interaction Logging

    After every interaction, write a summary Markdown file to the `internal-monologue/` folder in the repo root.
    - Filename format: `YYYY-MM-DD_concise-description.md` (e.g. `2026-01-15_update-readme.md`).
    - Content: a brief summary of what was requested and what was done.
    - Create the `internal-monologue/` folder if it does not exist.

DEBUGGING RULESETS

Recall that IBM Bob supports two rule scopes— Global and Workspace —and within each, mode-specific rules can also be applied. Bob may occasionally overlook Workspace-level rules. Global rules and agent-specific project rules tend to be followed more strictly.

If your rules aren't being honored as expected, send a prompt to the Agentic Sidebar such as the following: 

My project level rules in @/.bob/rules/basic_rules.md are not being listened to, please configure them properly

Submit the prompt and then proceed through the workflow. Bob may add the rules to each AGENTS.md file, apply them for a single instance, or take another approach.

docs.title: v. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Rules are plain-text files in .bob/rules/ that Bob reads and internalizes at the start of every conversation
  • These rules apply across all Bob Modes (but can be made Mode-specific if placed in particular rule directories)
  • Rules enforce consistent behavior without needing to re-introduce or repeat instructions with every session
  • Internal-monologue pattern rules give you an audit trail of Bob's actions across all sessions
  • Project-level rules are committed to the repository, making them available to the whole team
  • Global rules apply across every project on the machine

IBM Bob is endlessly malleable. You can tailor it behave the way you want, according to the pattern of work that fits your team. In the chapter ahead, you will explore the ways that Custom Modes can further shape Bob's behavior to every role within your organization.

docs.title: Custom Modes | Shaping Bob to every role
docs.text: MODULE 3 | TAILOR

docs.title: i. Shaping Bob to every role
docs.text:
IBM Bob's standardized, built-in Modes— Agent, Plan, and Ask —cover the most commonly found workflows and use cases that IBM's clients will encounter. But when pushing new frontiers and working at the scale of enterprise, there will inevitably be edge cases and bespoke cases requiring a tailored solution.

Custom Modes allow clients to define their own specialized agentic workflows with Bob: it combines a role definition, behavioral instructions, and a deterministic set of permitted tools. The net result for Bob clients is that, regardless of whether the end-user happens to be a product manager or a senior engineer, the Custom Mode "version" (persona) of Bob they interact with has been pre-tuned and shaped to how they actually work.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
For every Bob Mode, whether selected from the built-in Modes or client-tailored Custom Mode, is defined by a universal set of fields:

FIELD TYPE DESCRIPTION Slug Identifier Unique machine-readable name used to reference the Mode Name Display name Human-readable label shown in the Mode selector Description Non-deterministic High-level summary of what the Mode does Role definition Non-deterministic Defines how Bob should think and behave in this Mode When-to-use Non-deterministic Guidance for Mode orchestration (when other Modes should switch to this one) Custom instructions Non-deterministic Detailed behavioral instructions for how Bob performs tasks Tools Deterministic The set of tools Bob is permitted to use in this Mode

DETERMINISTIC VS. NON-DETERMINISTIC

The distinction between non-deterministic and deterministic fields matters when defining Custom Modes. The instruction fields guide Bob's behavior, but how Bob interprets and applies these fields is determined probabilistically.

The Tools field is different: it is strictly enforced. Bob is prohibited from using tools unless they are explicitly stated (permissioned) within the Tools field. For example, if a Custom instructions entry calls for use of a tool not inventoried within the Tools field, that instruction will be ignored. This property makes the Tools field— not the prose or contents of the user prompt —the real mechanism for constraining what Bob can do in a Mode.

QUIZ QUESTION - IBM BOB LEVEL 4

If you are planning to pursue IBM Bob Level 4 accreditation, what is rendered on-screen or returned within a console as a result of this step are likely referenced as part of a multiple-choice question. It is strongly recommend that you record to a notebook (for reference later) details about what is stated in this section about the Tools field, which is intentionally left OFF (and therefore the instruction is ignored.)

docs.title: iii. How to define and create
docs.text:
Custom Modes are created through the Mode settings panel in Bob IDE. You will have plenty of opportunity to try this yourself shortly in the hands-on materials. For reference, however:

  1. Click the Mode toggle button (may be labelled as Agent, Plan, or Ask at this time)
  2. From the expanded options, click the cog shaped icon to access Mode Settings
  3. The Bob Settings panel will open, make sure the Modes tab (left) is selected
  4. Click the + icon (top-right of the table of existing Modes) to Create new mode
  5. Fill in the slug, name, scope, custom instructions, and tool permissions
  6. Save the Mode
HOW TO TOGGLE DIFFERENT AGENTIC MODES

The label assigned to the Mode toggle button will change to reflect the name of the mode that the Agentic Sidebar currently has active. For example, if in the Agent mode, the toggle button will read as Agent. For the sake of clarity, when instructing you to change the Agentic Mode type, this documentation will refer to this toggle button as the Mode toggle.

You can scope a Mode to a single Project-level (stored in .bobmodes), or make it Global-level across all Bob projects and interactions. Creating a Mode through the UI generates a .bobmodes YAML file in the project root, which you can edit directly, commit to the repository so the whole team shares the same Modes, or use as a starting point for asking Bob to generate further Modes.

QUIZ QUESTION - IBM BOB LEVEL 4

If you are planning to pursue IBM Bob Level 4 accreditation, what is rendered on-screen or returned within a console as a result of this step are likely referenced as part of a multiple-choice question. It is strongly recommend that you record to a notebook (for reference later) details about where (the file or directory) that the Mode scope is stored for the Project-level.

docs.title: iv. A sample Custom Mode
docs.text:
To bridge the theoretical aspects discussed so far into a concrete example, consider a Mode built for Product Manager planning that aims to transform feature ideas into a structured, prioritized plan:

FIELD VALUE Slug product-manager Scope Project Instructions Transform ideas into a simple, prioritized product plan Tools Read, Edit, MCP (GitHub integration) Excluded tools Execute (terminal commands), Browser

The configuration of Tools speaks to the true capabilities of the Product Manager Custom Mode:

  • Read allows Bob to understand existing features and the current state of the code
  • Edit allows Bob to produce output documents, such as Markdown plans
  • MCP allows Bob to talk to GitHub (reading issues, linking plans to them)
  • Execute capabilities are excluded under the Excluded tools field because product work doesn't require running code (and limiting access to only as much as necessary is a security best-practice)

docs.title: v. Hands-on: Building a Product Manager Custom Mode
docs.text:
In the following steps, you will implement a real-world Product Manager Custom Mode end-to-end with Bob. To do so, you'll need to define its persona, grant it a deliberate set of tools to work with, and then put it to work against a real product manager scenario.

  1. Click the Mode toggle button and ensure it is set to Agent mode.

    HOW TO TOGGLE DIFFERENT AGENTIC MODES

    The label assigned to the Mode toggle button will change to reflect the name of the mode that the Agentic Sidebar currently has active. For example, if in the Agent mode, the toggle button will read as Agent. For the sake of clarity, when instructing you to change the Agentic Mode type, this documentation will refer to this toggle button as the Mode toggle.

  1. Click the cog icon to expose Mode Settings.

  1. The Bob Settings panel will open. Ensure that the Modes tab (left) is selected.

  1. Click the + icon (top-right of the table of existing Modes) to Create new mode.

    A new Create new mode panel will open within the Bob IDE.

  1. For the Slug field, enter the following:

    product-manager

  1. For the Name field, also enter the same details:

    product-manager

  1. For the Description field, enter the following:

    Turns fuzzy ideas into a simple, prioritized product plan with clear outcomes. Creates an MVP scope, user stories, success metrics, and a lightweight roadmap that a team can execute.

  1. For the Scope field, click the drop-down menu to expose more options. By default this value is set to Global.

    Change the value to the galaxium-travels project.

  1. For the Role definition field, enter the following:

    You are Product Manager Mode. You help define what to build and why. You clarify the user problem, propose an MVP, prioritize work, define success metrics, and produce simple, shareable artifacts (MVP card, roadmap, user stories, risks). You keep it practical and relatable for demos—minimal jargon, fast decisions, explicit tradeoffs.

  1. For the When to use (optional) field, enter the following:

    Use this Mode when you need to decide what to build (or build next), define an MVP, create a simple roadmap, write user stories/acceptance criteria, or define success metrics. Not for coding or deep technical architecture.

  1. For the Mode-specific Custom Instructions (optional) field, enter the following:

    Start by summarizing the request in 2–3 lines and extract:
• Target user
• Problem/pain
• Desired outcome
• Constraints (time, scope, dependencies)
2.  Ask up to 5 clarifying questions max. If answers are missing, make reasonable assumptions and label them clearly.
3.  Produce these demo-friendly outputs every time (keep each section short):
• MVP Card: Goal, User, Pain, In Scope (3–6 bullets), Out of Scope (2–4 bullets)
• Now / Next / Later roadmap (3–5 bullets per column)
• Top 5 user stories with “Done when…” (2–3 acceptance checks each)
• Success metrics: 1 Primary, 1–2 Secondary, 1 Guardrail
• Risks & open questions (2–4 each)
4.  Make tradeoffs explicit: if something is added to MVP, something else must move to Next/Later.
5.  End with a single recommended next decision the user should approve (e.g., confirm MVP scope or pick between two options).
6.  Keep language simple and relatable; avoid framework names unless the user asks (no RICE/PRD jargon by default).
7.  If helpful, include one small diagram (optional), e.g. a simple flow of the user journey.

    QUIZ QUESTION - IBM BOB LEVEL 4

    If you are planning to pursue IBM Bob Level 4 accreditation, what is rendered on-screen or returned within a console as a result of this step are likely referenced as part of a multiple-choice question. It is strongly recommend that you record to a notebook (for reference later) details about how the Now / Next / Later roadmap columns are organized, particularly how many columns are used when the roadmap is produced.

  1. Now comes the point where you can set limitations on which Tools that Bob (and the Custom Mode) are authorized to use.

    Toggle ON the following from the list of Available Tools. All other Tools should be left off (default).

    • Read: Allows Bob to read files in the workspace for this task
    • Edit: Allows Bob to edit files in the workspace for this task
    • MCP: Allows Bob to use MCP Server tools for this task

    QUIZ QUESTION - IBM BOB LEVEL 4

    If you are planning to pursue IBM Bob Level 4 accreditation, what is rendered on-screen or returned within a console as a result of this step are likely referenced as part of a multiple-choice question. It is strongly recommend that you record to a notebook (for reference later) details about which tools you toggled on from the Available Tools list.

    Collectively, these permissions grant the new product-manager Custom Mode the ability to read files within the project directory, edit those files, and utilize the open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP).

  1. Finally, press the blue Save button (bottom-right corner) to finish defining the product-manager Custom Mode.

  1. After saving, you'll be returned to the Modes sub-menu of the Bob Settings interface.

    Take note of the new tile for the product-manager Custom Mode that has appeared from the list of Modes.

    Connect to IBM VPN to access the marketplace

    Connection to the Bob Marketplace opens the doors to a tremendous amount of IBM and IBMer-publised Modes, Skills, and more tools that Bob can directly integrate with as part of its workflow. In order to view and access the Marketplace, ensure that your VPN connection to the IBM intranet is active.

  1. To the right of the search bar labeled Search Modes, click the drop-down marked as All.

    From the drop-down options, filter by Workspace modes.

  1. Within the Workspace modes list, the product-manager Modes appears alongside its description, confirming that the new Custom Mode was successfully created. These filters can be particularly useful when your Bob project space has accumulated multiple Modes — either ones you've authored yourself, or those that have been installed via the Bob Marketplace.

  1. Return your attention to the Agentic Sidebar session on the right side of the Bob IDE.

    Using the Mode toggle button, switch into the newly-defined product-manager mode.

  1. With the product-manager mode activated, copy & paste the following prompt into the session and press Enter to execute.

    What feature should we build next?

THROUGH THE LENS OF A PRODUCT MANAGER

As IBM Bob executes upon this ask and does so within the lens of the product-manager Mode you just defined, it will generate a detailed report about the current state of the Galaxium Travels project. It will first summarize the various functions and purpose of the application, identifying what has been built so far, and what Bob reckons (against its own understanding of such applications and coding best practices) remains missing from a robust and complete version of the service.

Summary Galaxium Travels is a working interplanetary booking app (React + FastAPI + MCP). The last major feature — seat classes (Economy / Business / Galaxium) — was fully shipped across all 6 sub-tasks. The product can now browse flights, register users, book seats by class, cancel, and view history.

MVP Card IBM Bob will define an over-arching goal of the work yet to be done— "Give travelers a complete post-booking experience — confirmation, trip summary, and smarter flight discovery" —and then reason out what components of that work should be treated as In Scope and Out of Scope. The purpose here is defining the immediate, low-hanging opportunities with immediate-to-short-term impacts on users (the Now and Next categories in the following table, respectively) versus those with longer-term-but-out-of-scope impacts (Later).

NOW NEXT LATER Booking confirmation screen (high visibility, low effort) Flight search & filter (origin/destination) Email / notification on booking "My Trip" detail expand in MyBookings Date-range filtering User profile page Backend query params for flight filtering Fare comparison across seat classes (matrix view) Payment integration Seat class badge in nav Saved/favourite routes Multi-passenger booking

Additional categories like Top 5 User Stories, Success Metrics, Risks & Open Questions, and Recommended Next Decisions are also captured within the product-manager Mode summary. All of these categories and metrics, of course, are particularly suited to an individual tasked with a Product Manager role in this context!

Continue exploring these details and asking additional prompts within the Agentic Sidebar if you wish, then proceed with the lab guide as we close out with Module 4.

docs.title: vi. Key takeaways
docs.text:
As the Tailor module wraps up, take a moment to trace back through your progression along the AI Maturity Curve: from conceptualizing IBM Bob as an Assistant; to being able to fully Delegate critical workloads to Bob; to now fully customizing a Tailored Bob workflow that adapts to users and use cases.

  • Custom Modes combine non-deterministic instructions with deterministic tool constraints
  • Tool restrictions are enforced, not suggested (they are the primary safety mechanism for Custom Modes)
  • Rules apply across all Modes (they are not overridden by custom Mode instructions)
  • Modes are created either through the UI or by editing .bobmodes directly
  • Project-scoped Modes are stored in .bobmodes and are committed to a repository

The final step in the journey— Module 4 | Scale & Extend —awaits.
